messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nabil is a 54-year-old software engineer who lives alone and works mostly from a downtown office where glass walls look out onto a busy street. Several months before seeking treatment, he was sexually assaulted by a man after leaving work late. He had stepped into an emergency-services access corridor beside his building to take a call, a narrow space where ambulance vehicles sometimes pulled through toward the hospital entrance a block away. A man approached, spoke with the confidence of someone used to being obeyed, and trapped him there. What remains most vivid to Nabil is not a complete narrative but a few sharply charged details: the rising wail of a siren somewhere close, the flash of emergency lights on the wall, and the sickening realization that he was alone with another man and could not get out. Since then, sirens, ambulances, and being alone with men have carried an immediate sense of danger that feels to him less like remembering and more like being thrown back into that corner.

In the first weeks afterward, Nabil told himself he should have seen it coming and should never have stepped into that corridor. He had come to believe the assault happened because of the way he acted, that he had made himself vulnerable by being polite, isolated, and inattentive. Alongside that self-blame was a bitter conviction that what happened was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. He did not feel rage in any full, freeing way; instead he spoke of being flattened, as though normal feeling had been switched off and might never come back. When he found himself constantly scanning doorways, listening for footsteps, and jolting as if something terrible were about to happen, those reactions seemed to prove his bleak conclusions. To Nabil, the fact that his body kept acting as though he were under threat meant something fundamental had been damaged, and it deepened his sense that he would never feel normal again.

His days gradually narrowed. At work, if an ambulance stopped outside and the siren echoed up between the buildings, he would shut his laptop, wait in the restroom until the sound passed, or leave by a back staircase to avoid the street entirely. If security staff or police officers were visible in the lobby, or if he saw uniforms near the transit entrance, he would stand frozen until he could find another route. He stopped going near the side corridor where the assault occurred, even when that was the quickest way from the parking garage to his office. When meetings ran late and he might be the only person left with another man in a conference room, he invented technical reasons to reschedule or insisted on keeping the door open. These habits made sense to him because he already felt he could be caught off guard anywhere; avoiding that block, authority figures, and situations with men was the only way he could reduce the constant sense that danger was about to break through.

Over time, those efforts to manage his fear began to organize his entire life. Nabil came to feel safe only in a few tightly controlled places: his apartment, his locked car, and a small workstation in the office when colleagues were nearby and the blinds were closed. Because he kept rerouting around the area of the assault and timing his arrivals to avoid police, building security, or emergency vehicle traffic, more and more ordinary parts of downtown took on the same charge. The sight of an ambulance near any curb, the sound of sirens from several blocks away, even noticing a uniformed person across the street could set off the same immediate alarm. His world had become something to scan continuously, and the more he organized himself around escape and avoidance, the more convincing it felt that danger was everywhere.

That shrinking of his life also fed the way he thought about what had happened. Missing team lunches, declining after-hours work, and leaving abruptly when sirens sounded left him ashamed and isolated, and in that isolation his self-blame hardened. He told himself that a stronger man would have reported it differently, fought back differently, recovered differently. Each accommodation he made to fear became, in his mind, evidence of permanent damage. He could see the unfairness of the assault clearly, especially when he passed the hospital district and thought about how public and unremarked the setting had been, but because nothing in his life had widened again, the unfairness curdled into the certainty that nothing would ever be put right.

By the time he sought help, his work had started to suffer. He was asking to remain fully remote, not because coding had become difficult, but because the office required too much vigilance: listening for sirens, checking who was in the hallway, calculating how to avoid being alone with men or crossing paths with uniforms downstairs. He came to treatment exhausted by how small his safe world had become. What frightened him most was not only another assault, but the possibility that this constricted, emotionally blunted version of himself was now permanent. What he hoped, though he said it cautiously, was that he might stop living as if every siren were the start of it happening again.
